Need for a Unified Export and Manufacturing Zones (UEMZ) framework to Strengthen 
India’s manufacturing and exports 
SHRI MASTHAN RAO YADAV B EEDHA (Andhra Pradesh):  Hon. Chairman, Sir, I 
wish to draw the attention of this august  House to the urgent need for a national 
Unified Export and Manufacturing Zones (U EMZ) framework to strengthen India's 
manufacturing base and export competitiv eness, with particular focus on the 
emerging industrial and port-led ecosystem in Andhra Pradesh.  
Sir, India has set an ambitious target of becoming a USD 5 trillion economy 
with manufacturing expected to contribute  25 per cent to GDP and exports crossing 
USD 1 trillion by 2030.  However, at present, manufacturing units, exporters, logistics 
hubs, SEZs, and industrial parks operate in silos and are governed by multiple 
authorities, approvals and compliance re gimes.  This fragmentation increases 
transaction costs, delays clearances and weakens global competitiveness, 
particularly for MSMEs, which account for nearly 45 per cent of manufacturing output, 
40 per cent of exports and over 110 million jobs.  
Many global manufacturing hubs, such as Integrated Industrial-Export Zones 
in East and Southeast Asia offer plug-and -play infrastructure, co-located customs 
clearance, testing and certification, skill  development centres and single-window 
approvals. These integrated ecosystems ha ve demonstrably reduced logistics costs 
by 20-30 per cent and accelerated export tu rnaround times. In contrast, India's 
logistics cost remains around 13-14 per cen t of GDP, significantly higher than the 
global benchmark of 8-9 per cent. 
Sir, Andhra Pradesh presents a compelling case for p iloting UEMZs. The State 
has a 974-kilometre coastline, six operatio nal ports and multiple Greenfield port 
projects. Major ports such as Visakhapatnam Port, Krishnapatnam Port and Kakinada 
Port collectively handle over 200 million tonne s of cargo annually. The State is also at 
the heart of nationally significant corridors  like the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial 
Corridor and the Chennai-Bengaluru Industrial Corridor. It is witnessing fresh 
investments in electronics, green hydroge n, renewable energy, food processing, 
petrochemicals, Defence manufacturing and sh ipbuilding. Sir, despite this, exporters 
in the region face multiple bottlenecks, sepa rate land parcels for factories and export

inspections and limited access to common testing and skilling infrastructure. A Unified 
Export and Manufacturing Zone, anchored around ports and industrial corridors, can 
integrate manufacturing, warehousing, logi stics, customs, skilling, R and D and 
MSME support within a single governance framework. 
Sir, I would like to ask the hon. Unio n Minister of Commerce and Industry 
whether the Government is considering a national UEMZ policy, and, if so, whether 
coastal and corridor-linked St ates like Andhra Pradesh will be prioritised for early 
implementation.

The Department of Fisheries, Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry 
and Dairying, Government of India has on 26 th October, 2022 accorded approval to 
the proposal of Government of Andhra Prad esh for construction of a fishing harbour 
at Kothapatnam in Prakashan District at a co st of Rs 364 crore with central share of 
Rs 80 crore under the Pradhan MantriMa tsyaSampadaYojana (PMMSY). The fishing 
harbour project envisages construction of breakwaters to create calm and tranquil 
basin, dredging, reclamation, quay wall s, internal roads, fish auction hall, 
administrative building, gear sheds, net mending shed, fishermen rest sheds, boat 
repair shop, restaurant, dormitory, secu rity guard room, compound wall, radio 
communication tower, water supply and sanitation facilities, ice plant, cold storage, 
effluent treatment plant, water storage facilities, drainage, electrification facilities, fire 
extinguishers and hydrants, greeneries an d landscaping etc.  The fishing harbour 
has been designed to provide safe landing,  berthing and allied facilities to a total 
fishing fleet of 820 vessels comprising 60 0 Nos of 9 mtr motorised vessels, 200 Nos

Concern over absence of tigers in Kawal Tiger Reserve at Adilabad  
District of Telangana 
SHRI S NIRANJAN REDDY (Andhra Pradesh) : Sir, I wish to address the concern 
over absence of tigers in Kawal Tiger Reserve of Adilabad District of Telangana.      
Sir, according to the All India Tiger Estimation of India (AITE) study conducted in 2018 
and 2022, there are no resi dent tiger populations in the Kawal Tiger Reserve, 
Telangana.
 While India’s overall tiger po pulation has reached 3,682 as of 2023, 
Telangana lags behind with an alarmingly lo w population of only 21 tigers. The Kawal 
Tiger Reserve, having a large reserve area of 2,000 sq.km., is reduced as a dispersal

by crossing the Pranahitha River.  However, due to loss of habitat, prey and 
poaching, tiger dispersal often results in conflict-related deaths. Such deaths are 
exacerbated by severe corridor fragmentat ion from encroachments, agriculture and 
infrastructure. Moreover, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) in a suo moto case of 
2024, observed that extensive tribal encroachments for podu cultivation has reduced

village relocation and corridor protection. Inadequate community engagement and 
slow adoption of technology continue to  undermine effective patrolling and tiger 
conservation.  Building on th e proven success of Project Tiger, I urge the Central 
Government to strengthen conservation at Kawal Tiger Reserve by issuing advisories

based reintroduction and monitoring fram ework, supported by clear accountability 
and annual performance audits.

Demand for ensuring access to essential narcotic pain medicines for

SHRIMATI KIRAN CHOUDHRY (Haryana):  Sir, I wish to raise an important issue 
concerning access to essential narcotic pain  medicines in hospitals, which directly 
affects patients suffering from cancer, se vere trauma, post-operative complications 
and those requiring palliative and end-of-lif e care. India has a robust legal framework 
under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, enacted to 
prevent misuse and illegal diversion. Howeve r, over the years, excessively stringent 
procedures and fear of legal consequences have unintentionally restricted the medical 
availability of opioid analgesics such  as morphine and fentanyl, which are 
indispensable for managing severe and persistent pain. Although Parliament took a 
progressive step through the NDPS (Amendme nt) Act, 2014 by introducing Essential 
Narcotic Drugs and a single-licence mech anism, implementation across States 
remains uneven. Many hospitals, especially at  the district and rural levels, continue to 
hesitate in stocking these medicines du e to complex compliance requirements and 
fear of penal action for minor procedural la pses. Further, limited training in pain

addiction and legal scrutiny have led to under-prescription, even when clinically 
indicated. As a result, effective opioid pain relief remain s confined to a few tertiary 
centres, leaving many patients with cance r and other chronic illnesses to suffer 
avoidable pain. World Health Organization has repeatedly emphasised that access to 
pain relief is a fundamental component of human healthcare. I urge the Government 
to uniformly implement the 2014 NDPS reform s, simplify hospital-level compliance, 
enhance pain management training, and stre ngthen palliative care, balancing misuse 
prevention with humane treatment.  Thank you.
